This study introduces a novel time series model, the TV-PARX model, designed to capture the evolving relationship between a time series and both its past values and external covariates. We provide consistent estimators for this model under a Markovian assumption and an irreducible, non-varying Poisson noise distribution. Our findings reveal that TV-PARX can effectively model complex dynamics, including non-linear behaviors, structural changes, and recurring patterns. We present our theoretical contributions in detail, along with an discussion on the validity of our results, an examination of alternative distributions and model variations, and an implementation of the TV-PARX model using a conditional Gaussian approach.

On November 13, 2020, a clear night in La Palma, astronomers used a Freskel imaged star field to calibrate their cameras, including the 0.6-meter Telescopio National de Chile (TNC). Without relying on absolute calibration, they employed a technique that links wide-field photometry to the narrow-field photometry from the telescope's guide camera to measure the night sky's brightness. Using this method, they measured the night sky's brightness across the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared spectrum, finding values of 20.53 +/- 0.05 mag arcsec^-2, 18.66 +/- 0.05 mag arcsec^-2, and 16.45 +/- 0.05 mag arcsec^-2 at 330, 550, and 850 nm respectively. They also measured the night sky's brightness in the near-infrared part of the spectrum, finding a value of 15.38 +/- 0.14 mag arcsec^-2 at 910 nm. To explain the night sky's brightness in the near-ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared parts of the spectrum, they used a model that considered airglow, scatted moonlight, and star light, determining a vertical aerosol optical depth of 0.072 +/- 0.012.

Numerous Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) samplers employing operator splitting techniques have been developed since the initial Verlet-based Method of Lines (MOL) implementation in NumPyORC in 2019. This study conducts an extensive simulation of the peptide bond of alanine dipeptide to determine the energy landscape of this system, comparing the PAD and TAD conformations. A key objective is to determine the optimal numerical scheme for HMC samplers in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy, testing various schemes including Stobi–Suzuki–Recknagel (SSR), Blanes–Oteo–Rosa (BOR), and a 4th-order custom scheme. A 2nd-order custom scheme is also assessed to evaluate the impact of increasing the HMC step-size numerical scheme order. Results from this study demonstrate that higher-order numerical schemes result in substantial computational efficiency improvements with minimal accuracy sacrifices, and the 4th-order SSR, BOR, and custom schemes exhibit nearly identical performance in terms of numerical efficiency and accuracy. The 2nd-order custom scheme exhibits slightly reduced numerical efficiency compared to the 2nd-order MOL, PAD, TAD, and 2nd-order SSR schemes but delivers more precise numerical integration results. Based on these findings, the 4th-order SSR, BOR, and custom schemes are recommended for use in HMC samplers employed in path integral molecular dynamics simulations to explore the phase and energy landscapes of complex biomolecular

This research delves into the potential biases present in image description datasets used for training training machine learning models and redefines them with more precise guidelines.  Without adequate guidelines, automatically generated images can pose a significant challenge for screening unsupervised learning datasets.  We propose new guidelines and create a modified dataset, CSDS, specifically for the training of classification machines learning models and the development of a classifier that distinguishes between describable and indecribable images with a 78.1% accuracy rate.  Our proposed description relevant to visually impaired users and available source code can be found on our project's website.

Optimizing the choice of vacuum expectation values in quantum field theory involves solving a set of equations known as Euler-Arnold equations. These equations have a polynomial structure and can be addressed using an adaptive spectral method, specifically the Legendre expansion. This approach is particularly effective given the polynomial nature of the problem. The Euler-Arnold equations are derived from the variational principle and are explained through a field-theoretic perspective, including an expression for the optimization loss that has a polynomial structure in quantum fields. This allows for an intuitive understanding of the gradient of the optimization loss, which also has a polynomial structure, through both variational and field-theoretic perspectives.

The interaction between a charm quark and a beauty quark in its ground state is examined herein using the potential model approach. By employing the Conson et al. constituent color charge model to determine how deconfined quarks charge each other, we calculate the modified ground state spectrum for this specific quarquark system. Our findings indicate that both attractive and repulsive forces from charge screening result in the production of new excited states within the $B\bar{c}$ system. These states include a 6.16 Gev $^1S_0$ bound state and a 7.54 Gev $^3S_1$ resonant state. Additionally, tensor and vector gluon interactions are shown to be responsible for the formation of $B\bar{c}$ meson excited states.

A sophisticated signal processing technique, known as wideband waveforming, has the ability to simultaneously serve multiple users in diverse areas by expanding the bandwidth allocated to each user. Although this method is effective, it also presents a complex challenge in optimizing throughput while ensuring fairness among the served users. In this context, we tackle the problem of maximizing fair and total throughput for all users accessed by a wideband waveforming system, subject to various constraints on beamforming and scheduling decisions. We demonstrate that calculating the maximum fair and total throughput is a computationally difficult task, as it is not polynomially related to the number of possible user areas. To overcome this challenge, we propose a fair-throughput optimization algorithm that can be executed in a reasonable amount of time, ensuring near-maximum fair throughput and satisfying all constraint conditions. Additionally, we derive a mathematical relationship between fair and weighted throughput, showing that the optimal fair-throughput allocation can be achieved by implementing a specific fair-weighting allocation pattern, all while maintaining a linear relationship between fair and sum-throughput optima.

Patching PDFs to ensure consistency across various scales is a key component of the successful mnemonics operator, as demonstrated by its performance on the Ames 70-TeV gauge and a number of other data points. The best results so far come from using the DGLAP mnemonics operator, combined with dglap evolution to handle scale changes, and a neural network-based pdfs generator to fit the data. Results are presented that show a clean70-teV gauge and a number of other data points can be accurately predicted using this setup, with a particularly strong result for the ames 70-teV gauge.

A novel combustingKennedyPergamotSampson linearized model is integrated within the numerical framework to investigate and predict the behavior of turbulent reacting flows, specifically methane-air flames, in a numerical manner. In a linear manner, we analyze flames in a numerical tubular reactor and a recirculating reactor configuration, focusing on low and high activation energy conditions, as well as varying strain rates. We utilize a Monte Carlo based approach to model the numerical reaction rate, and we employ a BrinkmanKerkhofkuijperdierkolemans model to incorporate turbulence, utilizing a direct numerical simulation method to achieve this. Our findings indicate that in a linear manner, both flames exhibit similar growth rates in a numerical extending flame zone configuration, yet when a recirculating reactor configuration is used with the same inlet conditions, we observe distinct behavior, particularly at higher activation energies. We utilize the linearized model to analyze and predict flame behavior in a reacting tubular reactor and recirculating reactor configuration, and we utilize a nonlinearKennedyPergamotSampson model as a baseline to achieve this. Our findings indicate that the linearized model, in a numerical manner, best suits the linearized framework, and we utilize this to calculate growing flames in a reacting tubular reactor and recirculating reactor configuration, obtaining results that align with the nonlinear model and existing experimental data.

Given the nonlocal nature of gravity, a nonlocal theory is proposed that is based on a constitutive relation which is shown to be relevant to observable quantities without relying on specific mathematical formulations. In a brief overview, nonlocal theory is summarized and various nonlocal models are reviewed that are based on local models, primarily aimed at resolving issues related to dark matter and dark energy. It is then noted that if a nonlocal theory is found which is based on a nonlocal gravity constitutive relation, it would be a major breakthrough, given the extensive array of nonlocal theories already established that are based on local gravity prototypes.

A notable trend observed in high multiplicity proton-proton (pp) collisions is the increased production of non-regular quark flavors, particularly the so-called $s$ and $ ar{s}$ quarks. A hypothesis suggests that a quark-gluon plasma might form within these collisions. Our research aims to investigate this trend using generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create modified particle production models at specific energies. Inputting existing experimental data on regular quark flavors and various energy levels, our evolved $N(s)  ar{s}}/N(p)  ar{p}}$ distributions match the observed trends. The proposed environment within high multiplicity pp collisions is found to be hot and dense, possibly inducing color screening effects similar to those seen in heavy ion collisions.

The equilibrium population of neutron star low mass X-ray binaries (LSXBs) is estimated using a dynamical model, focusing on recycling times, formation rates, and populations of both NSMps and NSLMXBs in the Galaxy. Key to the model are the FMps and FLMXB power spectra, as well as the IMF, CU, SN kick velocities, and Bi formation rates. Our results show that to balance the population of NSMps, the SN to CB bi formation rate should be between 0.01 and 0.1, regardless of whether OB bi formation is included. The observed deficit of expected recycled NSMps can be attributed to either higher SN to CB bi formation rates, slower neutron star migration due to reduced CU, or higher NSLMXB to NSMpx conversion rates, possibly due to beaming effects, disk outbursts, and metamagnetic outbursts. A detailed model of formation times, masses, and spins is required to further explore the potential of neutron star LSBXBs as progenitors of radio loud Mps and NSMpx populations.
A bipartite graph can be represented in a planar manner by dividing a vertex of degree three into two connected parts only if the graph is not three-part connectous, according to a new result.

Degrading a CPU's performance intentionally has been shown to enable more effective Flush-based cache attacks by reducing the time resolution of cache misses. While previous studies on CPU degradation focused on instruction cache eviction using Flush+Reload, this research delves further by exploring the data cache and presenting two novel techniques for implementing performance degradation in response to specific attack scenarios. The introduced method, called HyperDegrade, utilizes a branch predictor to induce performance degradation and achieves improved results compared to existing methods. HyperDegrade requires fewer traces to successfully pinpoint an application's location on the memory and achieves more accurate Brute-Force applications' address resolution compared to existing techniques. The technique has been found to contribute to better address resolution when combined with Branch Target Injection and has been shown to reduce the required trace count by a factor of 100 in comparison to existing methods, while also achieving a faster, more efficient Brute-Force process with a higher success rate.

A new variant of the traditional 2-brick model is introduced in this note, called the delta-brick model, which allows for a wide range of knotted structures to be reconstructed, including those formed by self-intersecting lines and different structures like bigons and gobras. By utilizing a modified version of the "erase an inverse move" used in previous research, a new move called the "diagonal move" is proven to be effective in simplifying any given knotted structure until the simplest form is reached, the same as the bigon for line graphs and the gobra for hypergraph models. This new variant allows for easy computation of graph models' native simplification, and an even more streamlined version of the move called the ultra-fast diagonal move is proposed, which allows for easier satisfaction of 1-brick model constraints while still guaranteeing that the move results in an equivalent configuration.

This paper focuses on collaborative learning in multi-agent systems, where
unprivileged agents can make informed decisions by observing the actions of
a privileged sensor-equipped agent. We investigate a scenario where the
privileged agent makes a sequence of decisions on actions, including
information release to nearby agents or exploration, with the goal of
maximizing overall benefit. We analyze two potential strategies for the
privileged agent, one based on the observed outcomes of actions and another
on the actions themselves. We establish bounds on the regret for these
strategies and validate their effectiveness through experimental results.

A Cartesian decomposition of a set involves subsets that partition the set in each dimension and whose product yields a product-based partition of the original set. This paper introduces two regular actions on the product space of the decompostion, and a additional action derived from two of the product-space partitions. We demonstrate that regular actions on the product space of two dimensions are fully characterized as either a single diagonal group or a combination of two diagonal groups. This result extends to higher dimensions recursively. As an application of these findings, we fully describe the edge-reachable component structure of the product graph of two decompositions.

A novel design for an interferometer, called the sloshing-Sagnac
interferometer, has been identified as capable of meeting the
enhancement needs for the Einstein@Home project.  By reconfiguring
the standard sifififififififififififififififififififififififififififififif{Sagnac}
interferometer layout, the sloshing design offers a expanded arm
length and a increased power recycling advantage over the
conventional design.  A theoretical analysis of the sloshing-Sagnac
interferometer demonstrates its potential sensitivity to be at least
as good as that of the traditional design, with a possible further
improvement of a factor of 1.4 if a multipass technique is
incorporated.  Consequently, the sloshing design presents a
cost-effective solution for enhancing the Einstein@Home project by
mitigating the need for expensive laser upgrades.  A step-by-step
plan has been outlined to transition from the current Sagnac
interferometer configuration to the sloshing design, including a
temporary setup and a gradual transition strategy, to ensure a
seamless upgrade process.

With the emergence of extreme wideband massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) technology, enhancing efficient random access (RA) protocols has become increasingly important. We propose an NOVR-XL based reciprocal pilot-based random access protocol specifically designed for XL-MIMO systems. Our proposed protocol eliminates the need for multiple retransmissions and reduces excessive blockages. We derive a closed-form expression to estimate the probability of successful access and validate it through Monte Carlo simulations. The results demonstrate that our proposed protocol outperforms existing protocols and achieves higher throughput. Moreover, we observe that XL-MIMO systems exhibit better performance compared to conventional MIMO systems.

A new ensemble technique that integrates n-gram-based machine translation models with a machine-learning based model has been proposed to improve machine translation and text summarization performance. The ensemble method uses a division of training data for the n-gram and neural language models, then combines their probabilities using optimal weights to obtain the final language model. The paper's results show that the ensemble technique outperforms existing methods by combining multiple machine-learning based models, and yields better performance in machine translation and text summarization tasks.

Optical Character Recognition has been used since 1989 to analyze votes cast in elections in Venezuela through a system known as TSE. These votes are entered on ballots scanned by a machine and the process is overseen by the voters themselves in a room called a tabulation booth. To ensure accuracy, the system's output is subject to review by the voters before the final results are submitted. However, the OCR system can make mistakes in reading handwritten data, which is common in vote tabulation. In an attempt to resolve these errors, an algorithm is used to monitor the process in real-time without delaying it. This algorithm, which works directly with the system's output, is noted for its simplicity and speed. To further improve the system's accuracy, a spell-checking mechanism is integrated that takes into account the context of the data. Once a minute, the system asks the voters if they agree with the corrected data presented on a screen. To verify the system's effectiveness, the paper compares the initial, raw results with the final, approved outcomes from the 12 May 2000 election in Venezuela.

A simplified atmospheric model for an Earth-like atmosphere is used to investigate the circulation patterns that may occur on Mars. When the Earth-like atmosphere is placed on the Martian gravity curve, large scale storms are triggered that bear a strong resemblance to observed baroclinic storms on Mars. A key wave formation is observed at a latitude of 45 degrees, which is consistent with the circulation patterns seen in baroclinic storms on Mars and the stormy atmospheres simulated in laboratory settings. The intensity of the storm is found to be greatly influenced by the strength of the Coriolis effect, which is enhanced by either decreasing gravity or moving to a colder environment. The findings suggest that baroclinic storms observed on Jupiter's moons, Europa and Titan, would also be expected given their low gravity and temperatures.

The Hankel path is an essential component of many complex analysis representations of special functions, including the Gamma function. Traditional numerical methods for calculating these functions on a computer require a complex representation that has the Hankel path as its contour of integration. We propose a new way of representing the Gamma function that uses the gamma data format and can be computed efficiently using deep neural networks. Our Hankel path-gamma network architecture is found to accurately calculate absolute and relative error values that are comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while also demonstrating our network's ability to meet specific mathematical identities and constraints. Hankel path representations of the Gamma function can be used to calculate and explore the complex scalar field behavior and asymptotic properties of the Gamma function, as well as related functions.

A linearized stochastic hydrodynamic method is integrated into the relativistic mean field approach to facilitate the simulation of quantum hydrodynamic fluctuations in its fully relativistic form. This method aims to enhance equilibrium Wigner function based hydrodynamic schemes by accounting for the nonlinear characteristics of quantum and hydrodynamic turbulence through a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic noise that is applied in a linearized manner during the course of a simulation. The linearized quantum and hydrodynamic noise is simulated using an implicit spectral method, and the resulting field is used to update the mean field parameters in a self-consistent manner. The resulting scheme is used to investigate the development of instability in an expanding relativistic fluid to determine its impact on forward-backward correlations in its non-equilibrium form. The results show that the nonlinear quantum and hydrodynamic turbulence can lead to significantly enhanced sideward flow and particle emissions, as well as increased low mass multiparticle correlations that are consistent with experimental data from the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider.

Teacher-Student learning frameworks have recently enabled deeply trained, large-scale teacher networks to assist in achieving enhanced performance in significantly smaller, lightweight student networks. Both Teacher-Student architectures and knowledge transfer techniques have significantly contributed to student network's ability to outperform a deeply trained teacher network. However, little is known about how Teacher-Student architectures, knowledge transfer techniques, input transformations, and target annotation resolutions impact the performance of a lightweight student network. In this paper, we focus on image classification to evaluate the impact of Teacher-Student architectures, knowledge transfer techniques, input resolution, and training targets on the student network's performance. We train both Teacher-Student architectures and standalone student networks on the ImageNet dataset and observe that knowledge distillation, where a teacher network emulates the teaching of a multi-branched, high-resolution teacher network to a single-branched, low-resolution student network, yields the most effective learning framework. We also observe that focusing on training targets that combine both raw images and teacher predictions at varying resolutions significantly contributes to a single-branched student network's ability to outperform the teacher network in terms of accuracy-size efficiency. Consequently, our best single-branched ResNet-based student network exhibits size-accuracy efficiency improvements over the current best Teacher-Student based, cyclic warm-up knowledge distillation, and single-crop training targets only, cognitive network architectures. Our single-branched cognitive network achieves size accuracy-efficiency gains that enable our 36MB cognitive network to match the

The problem of inferring a missing variable in a complex, high-dimensional graphical model is commonly resolved by a method known as message passing. A specific variant of this method, called Bucket Elimination, guarantees an optimal outcome when dealing with discrete and exact inference or optimization. This process works by systematically removing variables from the model in a sequence that is optimal. Building on this concept, we have developed an algebraic framework that extends Bucket Elimination to handle queries that are not fully specified, as well as to tackle issues related to model learning and structure selection. Within this framework, Bucket Enhancement serves as a unified method that can be used for inference, point estimation, and best-substructure approximation of variables. Moreover, Bucket Enhancement also provides an efficient optimization technique that can be used to explore the best substructure to focus on for more in-depth inference and optimization. This algebraic framework further enables a variety of existing inference and optimization algorithms to be combined and used together in a best-substructure best-first strategy. This strategy has been shown to exhibit best-substructure linear best-first characteristics to be exhibited by such combined methods.

We provide an explicit formula for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the centralizer $Z(n)(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of the central image of an $n$-dimensional subspace $n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ within the ambient space of matrices, as opposed to the vector space. The calculation is conducted by first obtaining the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the central image itself, and then utilizing an explicit formula for the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the quotient $P_{Z(n)}$ of the vector space. The explicit formula for the quotient's Hilbert-Poincaré series is derived through an application of Macdonald's relation and by showing that the central variety fails to satisfy Erman-Evans' relation. The explicit central variety Hilbert-Poincaré series is also verified through computation.

The paired-permutation test is an efficient testing method that can be used to detect relationships between two visual representations. An exact testing approach was developed with an efficiency of 99.3% compared to an established Monte Carlo approximation. The exact algorithm's improvement over the Monte Carlo approach is significantly better than a previous method by Bruner et al. (2011). The enhanced algorithm's efficiency is also compared to visual representation relations that are commonly used and found in the literature. The enhanced exact algorithm is available for use with the popular PyTorch and TensorFlow deep learning frameworks.

A notable trend showing identical transverse momentum ($p_T$) slopes for elliptic ($v_2$) and triangular flow ($v_3$) among various species of identified particles has been observed in heavy ion collisions. This pattern, contrary to the traditional hydrodynamic predictions, suggests a common dependence on transverse momentum ($p_T$) for the anharmonic anisotropic flows. To explain the observed $v_2$ and $v_3$ distributions among different particle types, a transport model called Art$QMD$ is employed for both proton-proton and heavy ion collisions at various energies. The model's outcomes align well with experimental data, except for the $v3n$ to $v3p$ ratio in heavy ion collisions at the highest energies. Notably, a stronger collision energy dependence of the $v_33$ to $v_22$ ratio in heavy ion collisions is predicted, in contrast to what was seen experimentally at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider.

This research tackles the challenge of detecting and estimating a target's location that is currently beyond the sensor's detection range, utilizing a sensor with a restricted field of view. To address this challenge efficiently, we propose an innovative point mass approximation technique specifically designed for detecting and estimating the target, which the analysis shows yields more accurate estimates of estimation uncertainty, compared to traditional methods that are easy to compute. It is also noteworthy that this new method results in optimal control strategies that are computationally feasible to implement. To validate our findings, we utilize a simulation environment that demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed technique in detecting the target, utilizing the sensor with a restricted field of view, by utilizing optimal control of the sensor's field of view that maximizes the probability of detecting the target within a given time frame. It is found that even with a control policy that is highly sophisticated and utilizes the full information about the system, the proposed technique is able to successfully detect the target, utilizing the sensor with a restricted field of view, by utilizing the control policy that maximizes the probability of detecting the target within a given time frame.

Optimizing game-playing strategies in team-based soccer robotics competitions presents a significant challenge. The vast action space and the difficulty in estimating action outcomes and their resulting rewards make this challenge even more pronounced. To address this, we propose using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to learn high-level strategies through self-play, and a feature set to predict the reward potential of actions, particularly in key game moments. Notably, causing the ball to go out of bounds, committing a foul, or gaining possession can sometimes be more rewarding than attempting a shot on goal in these scenarios. Our achieved strategy has been ranked second in the 2019 Robotics Soccer World Cup, and our publication is believed to be the first to use self-play to develop key moment strategies in robotic soccer competitions.

This paper describes an experimental physics setup that can be fully automated and controlled from a distance, specifically designed to address the demands placed by telework restrictions and similar situations in the future.  The setup, which includes a cryogenic detector, is accessible via a web interface that provides a live video feed of the experiment, allows users to control the setup, and enables the execution of diagnostic tests and automatic recovery procedures in case of malfunctions.  The system also features a chatbot that can answer frequently asked questions about the experiment and its operation.  The Web Interface described in this work has been successfully used by a significant number of physicists around the world during the COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrating the effectiveness of remote-accessible experimental setups in similar situations in the future.  The setup and its interface can serve as a foundation for the development of similar systems for other experimental physics setups that are similar in nature.

A new type of potential, which is slightly anharmonic, is introduced to the standard solitary wave system in a one-dimensional half-line domain. This potential, which is generated by an external force, is analyzed to determine its impact on the stability of the wave. Specifically, the paper proves that even under the influence of this anharmonic potential, the ground state of the system remains stable in terms of its properties and can be recovered over time. This is established through a series of estimates and the application of spectral theory, which shows that the system's linearized operator has a finite number of eigenvalues within a specific range and has a stable projection. Ultimately, a "global" approach is used to demonstrate that any disturbance to the system's properties decays over time, ensuring the system's stability.

The effectiveness of searches for exotic particles at colliders is heavily influenced by key properties, such as the decay length of any intermediate, long-lived neutral particles. For such particles that decay into detectable products with a significant delay, the optimal search strategy changes substantially based on the branching fraction and the specific decay distance.

A notable phenomenon in linguistics is the occurrence of semantic shifts within words over time. A prominent example is the use of "contextual variance," where a word's meaning changes based on the setting in which it appears, taken from its standard meaning. A well-known illustration is the shift in meaning of the word "big" when comparing its use in describing size versus importance. To fully grasp the significance of context-driven semantic changes, one might assume that substantial variations in meaning across different settings indicate a notable evolution in the language. Contrarily, our investigation reveals that significant jumps in a word's meaning in certain contexts can stem from the context itself, rather than a widespread shift in how the word is used. To validate this hypothesis, our study employed computational methods on a large vocabulary database, focusing on the evolution of the word "big" in the English language over the course of a century.

We found that although large-scale observations do not contradict the existence of a specific type of dark matter candidate, a light-heavy hybrid model is unstable at the particle physics scale. This is because the dark dark matter candidate, whose mass is estimated around $10^{-20}$eV and whose fraction of the total dark matter is between 10% and 100%, induces neutrino oscillations that result in an effective mass exceeding $10^{-29}$eV. This outcome conflicts with the findings on the absence of ultra-light particles.

Quantum dynamics of a vibrational state in a vibrational quantum system when subjected to a driven quantum system is driven by the state, and the state of the driven quantum system is driven by the vibrational state. We show that for a system/system when both are initially near to their their vacuum state, the state of the combined system/system after the driven quantum system is driven by the vibrational state can be approximately described by a coherent state, which is defined by the vibrational state and is the state of the driven quantum system that evolves linearly in a linear quantum system.

Quantum relational Hoare logic is used to evaluate how inputs and outputs are connected through a program's execution, especially when using side-channel communication, where the output is the encoded input. This paper introduces and verifies two side-channel communication programs with more complex input-output relationships. The first program outputs an encoded version of an encoded input, while the second program's output reveals information about specific characteristics of the input.

The precision of vector magnetic field maps is crucial for understanding solar physics, especially when analyzing large-scale phenomena like solar active regions. Traditional methods for deriving these field maps from spectro-polarimetric data often assume a completely magnetized pixel, an assumption that frequently fails due to weak magnetic fields in complex areas. This paper presents an innovative approach that explicitly factors in the magnetic fill fraction and employs a two-step process: initially estimating the magnetic field amplitude from polarization data and then accounting for fills that are filled magnetically through Bayesian inference. This new method is applied to a prominent vector magnetic field inversion, the Syntetic Vector Magnetic Field (SVMF), and shows significant improvements over conventional approaches, particularly in cases where magnetic fields are weak. By taking into account polarization signals that are often considered noise, this new method enables more accurate vector magnetic field maps and is expected to benefit future studies focusing on solar activity and flare prediction.

A Coxeter group can be represented as a system of reflections within a specific vector space, where a subset of these reflections forms a spherical area within a given sector. When we take into account a certain symmetry in the vector space, we can organize the remaining areas into distinct sections, or spheres, centered at each point on the sphere's surface. If the number of spheres in the area between two boundaries exceeds the number of spheres in a adjacent sector, adding a combination of spherical reflections in the adjacent sector to the current position in the system results in a smaller section. The following findings are obtained for specific examples of Coxeter groups, including $A_3$, $A_4$, $B_3$, $B_4$, $F_4$, $H_3$, $H_4$, $E_8$ and its subgroups, as well as certain nested structures within a $C_n$ group. The results provide the most minimal collection of symmetry reflections needed to reach all possible sections in the vector space for these examples. Additionally, the number of distinct sections within the section centered at the vector space's boundary can be calculated for groups $A_n$, $B_n$, $D_n$, $E_8$, $F_4$, $H_3$, $H_4$, $G(p,q,r)$, and $I_2(s)$, and a recursive formula is available for groups $G(p,q,r)$.

A curve whose osculating plane consistently intersects a fixed line is referred to as a curve associated with the line.  By examining such curves within the framework of the Peng-Sarnak geometry and the Iwamoto-Sano geometry, we can define the concepts of an osculating angle, curvature, and radius in these specific spaces.  Then, we can establish the existence of Bertrand curves in both the Peng-Sarnak space and the Iwamoto-Sano space.

Multi-task learning aims to combine various task objectives or functions to improve the learning process for each task. A key challenge arises from the choice of objective functions, especially when dealing with diverse tasks that may have different learning characteristics. A study was conducted to investigate the impact of using different objective functions on multi-task learning, particularly in natural language processing and vision tasks. The study used a shared model and compared common and under-used information theoretic measures, including Maximum Likelihood and KL Divergence, in multi-task learning. Results showed that commonly used information theoretic objectives may not always be effective, especially when combining multiple tasks, and that under-represented objective functions may not perform well compared to more used options. A new multi-task learning framework was proposed that gives equal weight to all tasks and aims to maximize all objectives, particularly in vision tasks, demonstrating significant improvements over existing methods. The study emphasizes the need to give equal consideration to all tasks and learn all tasks in multi-task learning, particularly in vision tasks, before using common optimization algorithms.

The task of synthesizing rules in natural language involves creating descriptions in the form of if-then statements that represent the relationship between different concepts. Our goal is to help different conceptions transform into one another. We developed a neural network model that can tackle this specific task and found that training the model on the hierarchical structure of different relation categories significantly enhances its performance compared to training it on just the level of relation groups. Additionally, we created a toolkit for this specific task and analyzed different if-then relationship types, including a summary of various concepts within the hierarchical structure of these relations.

This paper proposes a novel decision tree based method to predict videos from novel viewpoints within a multi-view setting. A key feature of this approach is its use of a dual representation, where videos are simultaneously represented in a Euclidean space and a non-linear decision boundary. This allows for an efficient novel view learning algorithm that uses only a subset of videos from the training set.

A graph $G=(V,E)$ is considered metric when the shortest path distance between any two nodes fully captures their relationship. In practical applications, directly measuring the distance between nodes can be challenging or costly, especially over large-scale networks. As a result, a modified distance metric has been proposed, denoted as $\delta_{t}(u,v)$, which captures the true geodesic distance between nodes within a network and assumes a fixed connection between a node and others within a specified threshold value $t$. This paper investigates the impact of truncating geodesic distances on the metric dimension of the resulting graph. It establishes bounds for the metric dimension of this modified graph and provides exact formulas for specific network structures, including paths, cycles, grids, and complete graphs. Furthermore, it derives exact formulas for the minimum node expansion required to recover the original geodesic distance within a specified accuracy.

A challenging problem in noisy environments involves accurately classifying sounds, particularly for medical environments where a patient's condition can be assessed through their heart sound. Traditional methods relying on clean sound data are ineffective in real-world scenarios, necessitating the use of complex systems that are costly to implement. In contrast, our proposed framework, called HS-SD, uses only clean heart sound samples for training and is capable of adapting to various noisy environments without the need for noisy training data. Testing was conducted using multiple heart sound datasets, including one with noisy training data and several with clean training data but varying heart sound conditions, to evaluate the proposed framework's performance. The results show that HS-SD outperpoints traditional methods, particularly in low signal-to-noise ratio environments, and achieves significant performance gains over standard pre-training methods such as GLD-Noise, especially when it comes to fetal heart sound samples.

A comparison is made between observations of extreme starburst galaxies and a simple theoretical model to determine the possible existence of a low-density molecular component, potentially in the form of a star-forming wind or a CGM reservoir, that may account for the unusual CI 159$\mu$m to CO emissions ratios seen in these areas.  A detailed examination is carried out on the relationship between CI and CO emissions, especially in highly active starburst regions, to explore the possibility that these galaxies are not as fully molecular as currently thought.  A low-density, partially molecular component, with a ratio of ionized to total hydrogen of approximately 10$^{-3}$ and a temperature of around 50K, is found to be consistent with all available CI and CO I spectral data and to cause a slight enhancement in CO emissions due to higher temperatures.  A simple model of a low-density, partially molecular wind or reservoir that matches the observed CI to CO flux ratios suggests that these components have a dust-to-gas ratio that is an order of magnitude lower than that of the main, dense gas disk.  Given the significant amounts of gas and dust required to form the outflows observed in these starburst regions, it is proposed that any winds or reservoirs are heavily shielded by self-gravity, making their detection through dust emissions difficult.  Future observations of CI lines from these regions, as well as efforts to detect self-gravity in outflows, are seen as essential to verify

This study investigates the velocity distribution of a second-class particle in an asymmetric exclusion process occurring in one dimension and equilibrium state. We discover that for time periods growing exponentially, the distribution consists of an exponential tail composed of mass points.

Epidemiologists use complex differential equations to model how diseases spread among populations. While fitting these models to data can yield precise estimates, there's a risk that the resulting models might not reflect biological reality. A Bayesian approach has been developed to guide the fitting process, ensuring that the resulting models are biologically feasible and that prior information about parameters is incorporated in a consistent manner. This method has been applied to an SIR model to analyze the spreading of COVID-2019 in various countries, with results that align with existing findings.

Observations indicate that as galaxy mass increases beyond approximately 10^10.3 solar masses, the NUV-r color becomes redder. This trend's origin remains unclear, though it may be influenced by changes in star formation activity and dust content within more massive galaxies. To investigate this, we utilized the massive galaxy sample from the DEEP2 survey, with 220 galaxies analyzed in detail and an additional 400 identified as candidates, covering a wide mass range. Spectroscopic confirmation of the candidates is currently underway. Our findings reveal that more massive galaxies exhibit less excess growth at the halo center compared to those with lower masses, consistent with theoretical predictions. When comparing galaxies of similar mass, those with higher densities show slightly redder colors, likely due to differences in the gravitational potential affecting gas dynamics and cooling. The observed correlation between color and mass aligns with the relationship between color and velocity dispersion found in spirals, as velocity dispersion is a strong indicator of galaxy mass.

A multi-task learning approach is presented that enables a sentiment classification model in a low-resource language to align with existing sentiment annotations in a high-resource language, without requiring any additional training data in the low-resource language.

A stellar survey conducted by the Kepler mission has identified a intermediate-mass star with a rapidly rotating equator, KIC 9267654, whose inner regions may be experiencing a counter-intuitive slowdown in rotation. To determine the underlying causes of this profile and assess its significance, we have analyzed the star's spectral characteristics, estimated its rotational velocity, developed a theoretical model, and considered various potential explanations. Although our data is limited, it suggests that KIC 9267654 is an 1.8 solar mass star with a 14-day rotational period. Based on the Clayton-Kumachew theory of angular momentum conservation, we determined that the star's rotation profile should be significantly steeper. We have examined three possible reasons for the observed profile: the presence of an inflated radius, the expulsion of the star's outer layers, or the acquisition of angular momentum from the surrounding corona. We found that even slight outer layer expulsion or corona inflation could account for the unusual profile, suggesting that minor factors can have a substantial impact on the rotation of the star. Additionally, we assessed the stability of the rotated profile and the conservation of the star's chemical composition in case of outer layer expulsion.

Recent surges in misinformation dissemination on social media platforms have compelled advanced detection systems to be implemented more effectively. Although machine learning-based methods have shown success in fact-checking, they fall short in addressing unforeseen misinformation trends. Conversely, symbolic approaches can fact-check information but are limited in analyzing complex fake news structures. Our proposed MetaFEND system integrates the strengths of both learning and symbolic methods to facilitate end-to-learning fact-checking on fake news. Utilizing automatic theorem proving to analyze suspected fake news and utilizing machine learning to identify factual evidence on the trending topic, our MetaFEND system demonstrated its efficiency. When tested on the Weibo dataset, our system achieved a 92.6% precision rate in identifying factually uncertain topics and successfully fact-checked the entire dataset. Additionally, the system publicly available at https://github.com/XuechenLi/MetaFEND.

A quaternary Golay complementary array pair is a special arrangement of numbers that can Feature a specific property where the sum of their autocorrelations has a zero peak. Determining the minimum length for this property in lengths 12 through 20 requires lengths of 16 and 20 to be feasible. Feasibility is confirmed when quaternary Golay complementary arrays pair with specific patterns can be formed, which in turn requires the existence of Golay complementary dyad pairs within those patterns. We demonstrate that lengths 16 and 20 are feasible by providing configurations for the required patterns.

This work presents a novel approach combining AI techniques for automatically identifying and segmenting significant areas in medical images, specifically for CT scans. Unlike previous methods that used CNNs, which struggle with thin-walled, gas-filled regions on images, this proposed technique utilizes a different type of neural network, the CRN, which effectively handles such areas. In addition to automatic segmentation, this method can also utilize external information, such as physical properties and analytical equations, to enhance accuracy. The results show that this approach not only matches but also provides point estimates of analytical solutions for regions identified in images, making it a valuable tool for medical imaging analysis.

This paper proposes an innovative, combined unsupervised and supervised framework for manifold learning called FSDM. The framework integrates feature selection and dimensionality reduction to better understand and process high-dimensional data. The initial step involves an unsupervised phase that utilizes deep autoencoders to preprocess the data, followed by a supervised phase that employs FSDM to finalize the learning process. FSDM focuses on capturing the intrinsic structure of the data by modeling the probability distribution of a low-dimensional representation. The representation is further refined through probability mass function fitting, cluster identification, and clustering optimization using FSDM. The proposed framework is validated through multiple experiments on real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance compared to other methods.

Large-scale language models that have been trained on extensive knowledge graphs in their structured form are becoming increasingly relevant to both the AI research community and the industry. While models pre-trained on traditional, unstructured text-based corpora have demonstrated their effectiveness in various natural language processing tasks, the potential of knowledge graphs as a training material for pre-trained models has not been fully explored. Our work fills this gap by developing a new, self-supervised learning framework called TripleTune, which enables large-scale language models to excel on downstream tasks involving structured knowledge graphs and facilitates the adaptation of prominent knowledge graph-pretrained models to fit specific tasks. Through triple-based training on vast knowledge graphs and the creation of several knowledge graph-pretrained variants, our TripleTune framework shows that language models can successfully adapt to various downstream tasks involving structured knowledge graphs, including fact verification, explanation, and reasoning. Furthermore, our knowledge graph-pretrained models outperform traditional text-based pre-trained models on multiple downstream tasks and can be readily applied using a frame work called Elastic Weight Consolidation, enabling models to learn new tasks without compromising previously acquired knowledge.

A new non-linear charge parameter for Yang-Mills fields is introduced and its impact on black hole physics is examined. The field equations are modified in a minimal way, and solutions are found numerically for both Schwarzschild and Reissner-Nordstrom black holes. A shadow imaging method is adapted for the non-linear fields. It is discovered that the non-linear charge affects the thermal profile of black holes but has little effect on the shadow radius. It is also found that the non-linear charge affects the calculation of the thermal profile of naked singularities as well. A threshold is established where thermal equilibrium becomes impossible for certain black hole configurations. The results obtained are primarily influenced by the specific thermal profile model used rather.

Quantum phenomena such as entanglement and its increase are essential for secure communication and the advancement of quantum networks. These properties are hard to verify through traditional measurement methods but are easily observable through optical tomogram-based quantum state representations, which are essentially probability distributions of particle positions. Our research demonstrates that even nonclassical state transformations, such as entanglement enhancement, leave detectable traces in optical tomograms. We use particle position probability distributions to predict nonclassical effects and calculate the speed of such effects to be at least on the order of light speed, confirming them by comparing experimental and theoretical optical tomograms. This research indicates that optical tomograms can not only depict nonclassical states of matter but also manifest and reveal such nonclassical properties and transformations, including those occurring at least at light speed. Consequently, particle position probability distributions and their derivatives, when considered collectively, can serve as a nonlocal and relativistically consistent measure of nonclassical effects such as entanglement and its increase, making them suitable for quantum networks and communication purposes.

A measurement of the branching fractions for the $B^0_d$ meson decays into either the $K^{*0}\bar{K}^0$ or the $K^{*0} ar{K}^{*0}$ state has been made based on data from 3.9 to 4.7 TeV center-of-mass energies, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 264 $^{-14}^{+25}$ $\mu$b$^{-1}$, as collected by the LHCb experiment. The branching fraction Rats$^{*0}\bar{K}^0$ is measured to be (7.33 +- 0.28 +- 0.24 +- 0.20)x10^-3 and the branching fraction Rats$^{*0} ar{K}^{*0}$ is found to be (6.77 +- 0.34 +- 0.27 +- 0.19)x10^-3, with the uncertainties being statistical, due to luminosity and cross section, as well as from simulation and tagging efficiencies, respectively.

To reconstruct the lattice of submodules for a module's composition multiplicities, starting from its type, we focus on a multiplicity-free module over an algebra of dimension seven. By incorporating the structure of its nontrivial submodules, can we predict the resulting lattice of submodules?

A key finding in harmonic analysis shows that recurrent operators, including those found in physics like the Helmholtz operator, do not affect the condition where biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space are considered minimal.
This paper proves a Boolean closure property for languages recognized by machines with a p/q state model and goes further to establish a connection between these languages and automata theory.

This paper presents a unified framework that extends the Boyd-Grinstein-Lebed (BGL) approach to the K*0 to gamma transition form factors, incorporating the Caprini-Lellouch-Neubert (CLN) method. By integrating both perspectives, we derive new constraints on the shape of form factor regions that were previously undefined. These additional constraints when applied to the available data imply significant modifications to the BGL interpretation and align more closely with the CLLN curve in the absence of experimental discrepancies.

A dynamical system is considered locally stable when a bounded initial region remains bounded over time. Conversely, even minimal perturbations leading to exponential divergence within a short period indicate an unstable system. We define an unstable system one where exponential divergence occurs, specifically when the Lyapunov exponent is positive. Although many machine learning models have demonstrated capacity for controlling complex systems, the efficacy of such control is often short-lived due to the inherent tendency of many systems to expand their range when perturbed. In this context, our model proposes using reinforcement learning for stabilizing systems by teaching them to counteract exponential divergence. We define an unstable system as one that experiences exponential divergence when a particular action is taken, specifically when the_lyap_ exponent is greater than zero. Our research indicates that an effective action exists whenever a system is deemed unstable, with the exception of rare scenarios where the system is destined to wind down on its own. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed model through successful tests on various systems, including the double pendulum, cart pole, and car, among others.
This article defines angle functions in broader spatial contexts and derives conditions for conformal embeddability for specific spatial models.

Relying on TPC's integration with existing GPNP and PGNP frameworks, we anticipate its relevance to existing guarantees against PNPD and NPDd models, as well as PNPE, NPE, and NPEE models. Consequently, we anticipate that the certified accuracy against PNPE, NPE, and NPEE models, as well as PNPD, NPDd, and NPD EE models, should theoretically equal or exceed the certified accuracy against PNPD, NPDd, and NPD EE models. Our experimental results support this hypothesis, showing that adding 0.01 seconds to the certification time for point cloud models against PNPD and NPDd models would result in the models also being certified against PNPE, NPE, and NPEE models.

High cognitive costs in software development often lead to uncorrected bugs, especially in complex projects. Although proof assistants have gained popularity in research areas with significant cognitive costs, UNMATED I (test/automation environments) have seen rapid adoption in engineering and applied fields. To help developers efficiently identify and fix bugs in projects of any size, we created UNMATED I, a fully automatic testing environment that integrates with any proof assistant, with a focus on Coq but also supporting Chameleon and Assiut. A groundbreaking algebra of cognitive costs has been developed to optimize tests and minimize costs in projects of any size within the testing environment. As of now, over 100 instances in GitHub have benefited from UNMATED I, with a 93% success rate in automatically identifying and fixing bugs discovered by the testing environment. To further demonstrate the testing environment's effectiveness, a cognitive costs optimizer in (UnMate) has been made available online at https://unmate.github.io/ and the code is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/UnMate/UnMate.

G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles on geometric objects represent modified, non-trivial crystalline extensions of the base field whose Matier-Murphy algebra is isomorphic to the object in question. In this paper, we examine the connection between G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles and reducing crystalline extensions modulo a prime number p. As an example, for triangular algebra A = tri(BO), G_K-Artin-Scheier cocycles corresponding to a function f in the ring of integers of a field matching the field of numbers corresponding to p, are shown to be equivalent to triangular extensions of the base field whose Matier-Murphy algebra is isomorphic to the object in question in question (A_a, a, mu), where a is the image of f modulo p and mu is the projection of the extension modulo p.

Engineering critical composite structures like aircraft wings prioritize safety by quickly detecting and addressing potential damage. Traditional high-fidelity simulations, while accurate, are computationally expensive and not suitable for real-time damage detection applications. This issue is particularly relevant for advanced materials like self-sensing carbon fiber reinforced polymers (CFRPs), which can monitor their condition through embedded sensors using techniques such as electrical impedance tomography (EIT). To enhance the precision of damage imaging in these materials, a graph neural operator (GNO) based model was optimized through a competitive genetic algorithm (GA). This process involves training a minimal CFRP-FE model with a coarse mesh, which is then used to estimate the physical properties of a more detailed version of the same model. When applied to a self-sensing composite wing with a fine mesh, this approach can accurately detect and visualize damage, even in complex scenarios. Given the importance of engineering composite structures in applications like aircraft wings, this method presents a highly effective way to improve the capacity of these structures to detect and address damage with precision.

Vector calculus has been re-examined in this research with modified gradient, curl, and divergence operators yielding a rich geometric framework. This new framework results in a number of integral identities proven using geometric vectors and a connection to the Foku-Martin boundary class of analytic functions. Many of these identities are not available in the existing framework and offer a fresh perspective on the Foku-Martin class.

Action on trees by a group is an effective way to study the group's properties, especially for the action to be geometric. A notable example is the action of right-angled Artin groups on trees. A subgroup of such a group is known to action on a minimal tree in a geometric manner, with its properties heavily influenced by the structure formed by its stabilizing patterns. A right-angled Artin group's subgraph being or not separable, determines whether the corresponding subgroup's action on the tree is finite. A subgroup being the free product of other subgroups is easily identified, as it corresponds to a subgraph that is also a free product of other subgraphs. However, determining if a subgroup's action on the tree is convex or can be represented as a free product is a more complex problem, as it involves analyzing the subgraph's structure in a similar way.

This paper Nested Neumann algorithm is proposed for solving inverse problems with a specific focus on structural parameters that are non-linear in nature. The method combines the advantages of the Level Set method and the Shape Gradient approach and can be initialized using a rapid initial estimate provided by the Multiphysics Level Set method. The Nested Neumann algorithm is designed to overcome limitations related to local minima and ensures a smooth convergence by adjusting the inception depth of the Multiphysics Level Set. A theoretical foundation is established that links the convergence rate of the Nested Neumann algorithm to its inception depth and a constant that is positive in nature. The proposed algorithm is validated through two test cases that involve heat conduction and acoustic wave problems with a non-linear geometric configuration.

We establish new, near-optimal bounds on the required communication overhead for contextual linear bandit learning. Notably, we demonstrate that even with no prior knowledge about the context, efficient learning can be achieved. Furthermore, we show that understanding the context can significantly reduce the need for communication. Specifically, if the situation involves Gaussian contexts, the total communication needed is bounded by a value related to the dimension and probability of rare events. Similarly, in situations with polynomial context distributions, the value is boundable by a function of the degree and constant of the polynomial. We also provide optimal bounds on initial and total communication needs when context distributions are known. Notably, our results show that if the context distribution is uniform, no communication is required initially.

A key uncertainty in protoplanetary disk research is the connection between
chemical and physical processes at the micron scale, particularly the growth of
silicate particles and its impact on radiation transport. To address this, a
novel numerical model has been integrated into a global protoplanetary disk model
to assess the effect of silicate particle growth on disk evolution, focusing on
the outer regions beyond 5 astronomical units. In these areas, gas accretion is
dominant and dust settling enhances particle growth. Without setting assumptions
about particle sizes, the connection between optical depth and height above the
disk midplane can be used to simulate the effect of silicate particle growth on
disk cooling efficiency. The results show that as silicate particles grow from
0.1 to 10 microns, the rate of cooling in the disk's surface decreases by an
order of magnitude. This leads to a thermal buoyancy problem, causing the disk
to stay puffed up with a steeper vertical gradient. However, with larger particles,
re-settling occurs and the disk becomes flatter. Given the rapid rate of gas
accretion in outer disk regions, achieving significant particle growth requires
time, which improved cooling efficiency can provide. Therefore, this newly
proposed mechanism of dust-driven evolution can serve as a self-sustaining
cycle that affects the outer disk's architecture and chemistry, particularly the
formation of planets and their subsequent migration.
This paper proves a bound on the dimension for harmonic functions with limited growth on gradient shrinking Ricci solitons. It also establishes the infinite dimensionality of such a function space.

Data classifiers trained using deep learning techniques are vulnerable to maliciously crafted inputs, known as backdoors, which appear normal but trigger specific actions when identified by the backdoor trigger. Most research on learning backdoor triggers has focused on static triggers, which are fixed and unchanging throughout the input, whereas real-world backdoor attacks are often dynamic, with triggers that can change with each compromised individual. So far, implementing a dynamic backdoor in various classification tasks has been challenging and required access to the target classification system. We have discovered a highly effective method to classify images with real-world dynamic triggers that change location and appearance, requiring no knowledge of the target system and works even with triggers appearing in frames of a video. This is made possible by a universal detector that helps embed distinct triggers for different individuals while not degrading the classified inputs, and which works better than current methods in various classification tasks including image and video classification. Our proposed system, called DynamicBND, achieves this with minimal impact on the accuracy of classified inputs and is shown to work effectively in face and object recognition tasks on the MNIST, FMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CUB-200-2011 datasets.

A learning task involving a training dataset is performed collectively by a group of machines in this paper. When the training dataset is kept on each machine and not centrally stored, and the machines are far apart and have slow, unreliable connections, this task becomes challenging. We propose a new method for the learning task that can be efficiently carried out by the group of machines, despite the difficult communication conditions. The method uses a series of steps where only a few pieces of random data is shared between the machines, and we prove that after a reasonable number of steps, the machines can accurately train a linear model. The method's performance is tested and found to be effective in various testing scenarios.

Semi-supervised learning has the advantage of utilizing a large dataset that contains mostly unlabelled data, which is especially beneficial in the field of medical image segmentation where obtaining labelled data is expensive and time-consuming. In a recent study, the purpose was to develop a new method called Integral Mix, which serves as a regularization technique for semi-supervised learning by using an analloric mixing approach based on ancalculating labelled and unlabelled data points between adjacent points in a coordinate space. The mixed curriculum, which is an sequential learning plan, is then derived from the analloric mixing to progressively learn the segmentation task in a semi-supervised setting. To evaluate the effectiveness of Integral Mix, the method was tested on several medical image datasets including the ACDC, Heart, and PaMD datasets for cardiac and pulmonary medical image segmentation. The analloric mixing approach proved to be especially effective in a semi-supervised learning setting, where the Integral Mix outperformed existing mix regularizations by a large margin, especially in cases with a small number of labelled samples.

Quantum correlations within a single particle's entanglement have been shown to exhibit nonlocal behavior and enable quantum steering in complex systems consisting of multiple parts. This phenomenon is made possible by single particle entanglement when the system's parts are distinguished by different points in space or by different quantum properties such as spin or polarization. In a systems with parts differentiated by spatial properties, single particle entanglement has been shown to exhibit nonlocal effects and enable quantum steering in a way that is harder to achieve than in systems where parts are spin or polarization based. This is because single particle entanglement in systems consisting of just one quantum property based part is shown to exhibit nonlocal behavior and enable quantum steering. This research is supported by various funding sources including the German Science Foundation and the Austrian Science Fund.

The integration of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) and Blockchain (BC) represents a transformative approach to enhancing security, privacy, and real-time information sharing within vehicular networks. Although the combination of IoV and BC offers significant advantages, the inherent limitations of BC in terms of storage, retrieval, and verification present challenges that need to be addressed. In an effort to overcome these challenges, a novel BC-enhanced information sharing protocol has been proposed, leveraging a centralized server for data caching and employing cryptographic techniques to ensure privacy and integrity. The protocol utilizes smart contracts to automate the process of verifying, retrieving, and updating information, thereby optimizing BC's limitations while improving security, privacy, and real-time information sharing within the network. Performance evaluations through theoretical analysis and simulations demonstrate the protocol's effectiveness in enhancing security, privacy, and information sharing within the network.

This research presents a new hardware-based recurrent neural network lattice called the Forward Differece Harmonic Transform Long Short Term Memory, integrated within the existing high-performance hardware frameworks for reducing storage and computation in deep learning systems. The FDHT LSTM hardware design is specified at the system level with a performance evaluation using a tensor-based optimization technique called simultaneous diagonalization. The created model is named the FDHT-LSTM lattice which is presented as an alternative to the traditional THT-LSTM model in hardware design. The FDHT-LSTM architecture is found to be both computationally efficient and well-conserved in the hardware environment when using the simultaneous diagonalization tensor optimization strategy. The FDHT-LSTM design shows improved throughput and energy efficiency in comparison to the existing high-performance hardware lattice called the TPETL and TT lattice in deep learning systems which are used for storing and computing word context vectors in natural language processing and machine translation systems, with gains of 1.37 bits per second and 0.02 nano Joules per second in throughput and energy efficiency respectively when using a state-of-the-art machine translation system named the MTEDF system.

The Bateman-Horn Conjecture's polynomial analogue is proven for specific generators in a function field of a finite field, where the generic Galois group is identified as the symmetric group $S_n$. This result in function fields supports and aligns with the application of group theory in this context.

This article addresses the Schrödinger equation's solutions in a bounded domain with a concave boundary, focusing on the impact of the boundary in a semi-classical context. We demonstrate that solutions can experience a sudden increase in amplitude, or 'blow-up', when initial conditions meet the boundary in a specific way. This result is notable as many techniques that prove blow-up in unbounded domains, like those for the Schrödinger equation, don't apply in this context. The proof relies on a new estimate for the solution's $L^q$-norm that emerges from the equation's part with the boundary and the choice of a diffusing operator that doesn't account for the boundary.

This paper introduces a transformation from commutative algebra in a given characteristic p to the same algebra in characteristic zero, the standard method which involves extending to the fraction field and moving to characteristic zero by way of the Frobenius endomorphism. Since this technique only applies to unramified extensions of the integer ring of a given field K, we propose an alternative flattening technique that applies to both ramified and unramified extensions.

Decision-making under uncertainty is a key area of machine learning research. One prominent approach uses utility functions to guide actions, but its application in hypothesis selection has not been extensively studied. We propose using utility functions to guide action in hypothesis selection, drawing on the information theory concept of mutual information and the decision theory framework of value of information. To do this, we developed three novel value of information metrics for guiding Bayesian optimization. Since there is no guarantee that the optimal action can be found, we examined three common strategies and tested them in scalar and multi-scenario problems, including image processing. Our experiments used a surrogate model based on Gaussian processes and a hypothesis set consisting of sharp boundaries, smooth curves, and shapes. The results show that using utility functions to make informed decisions is an effective approach, particularly when combined with the exhaustive search strategy and the value of sample information metric.

Discourse markers, despite their widespread use in daily communication, present a challenge in accurately determining their meanings due to the contextual variability and lack of established standards for describing their relationships. To address this issue, our team has created DiscSense, a new dataset consisting of 5,000 segments of text that have been annotated with their semantic relationships as defined by the Prosody taxonomy. If not considering the subcategories, there are 13 distinct semantic relationships identified within DiscSense, which can be further broken down to a total of 21 categories when including more granular levels. It's worth noting that DiscSense is the most extensive collection of data available on discourse markers specifically focused on the semantic relationships between them. To verify the quality of our dataset, we conducted a zero-shot evaluation on various tasks including recognizing the patterns of discourse, understanding its structure, and determining its semantic meaning. The results indicated that pre-trained language models have a deficit in discursive understanding, although it can be improved through further training. To facilitate the analysis of semantic relationships between markers, we have made the DiscSense dataset publicly available at https://discsense.github.io/.

Due to the lack of inhomogeneous quantum Affine $S$-matrices corresponding to non-simple non-trivial twists, we define and examine a generalized version of the basic quantum Affine $S$-matrix related to a twist that is a generalized version of the simple Jordanian twist. We define the twist that is a generalized version of the basic quantum Affine $S$-matrix and verify that it satisfies the multiplicative property. In addition, we derive the quantum Affine $K$-matrix that is related to the twist that is a generalized version of the basic quantum Affine $S$-matrix and verify it meets the required condition.

This work presents a novel, symbolically-based decision procedure for analyzing regular expression inclusion. We begin by introducing Brzozowski's derivative operator and its generalized version for regular expressions, which we fully demonstrate as a decision-making tool for checking regular expression equivalence. Building on these generalized Brzozowski derivatives, we develop a specific rewriting algorithm that serves as a decision procedure for determining if one regular expression is encompassed by another, and we also provide a Grammatical representation of this operator as a Datalog rule.

We examine the properties of geodesic operators within both AdS$_{2}$ and AdS$_{3}$ spacetimes, with a particular emphasis on understanding the representation of conserved current conformal field theory blocks in CFT$_{2}$ when expressed using only AdS$_{2}$ geodesic operators. Our analysis reveals that, analogous to the situation with energy density operators, the creation of higher spin conserved current operators requires the incorporation of additional, non-geodesic components. Furthermore, we explore the connection between the operator within the AdS$_{2}$ spacetime and its counterpart in the AdS$_{3}$ spacetime for a specific configuration where AdS$_{2}$ is embedded in AdS$_{3}$.

On 2024-05-20, the lobster-eye optics system consisting of semi-spherical microlenses was reoriented by 90$^\circ$ around the vertical axis. Following this adjustment, a cross-shaped shadow cast by four extended sources positioned outside the lobster-eye optics system exhibited distinct changes. Notably, two of the visible segments of the cross disappeared, while the remaining two segments rotated and swapped their right ascensions by 180 degrees. This phenomenon demonstrated the power of slightly reorienting the lobster-eye optics system to identify and characterize its various segments. Moreover, it highlighted the value of slightly rotating the lobster-eye optics system to map the sky more efficiently, as well as the necessity of doing so to account for the varying fields of view of each lobster-eye optics system segment.

A key parameter in cosmological simulations is the amplitude of initial scalar perturbения, denoted as S2. An accurate halo mass model that can predict the mass of dark matter halos using a density-only initial condition is highly valuable. We developed a neural network-based halo mass model called HMTree-Pi, which takes only one-dimensional median halo properties and no real-space information to predict the dark matter halo mass. When used with initial conditions from a dark matter-only simulation for the FairBBox project, with a specific set of halo properties as input and no information about the environment, we found that using only initial density to predict the dark matter halo mass results in a negligible increase in halo mass underestimation. This occurs only when initial condition models with a very high amplitude of initial scalar perturbения, with a threshold of 10^-2, are used. At this threshold, the model shows a more significant bias in the transition of halos from bound to unbound state, as opposed to models with a lower amplitude of initial scalar perturbения, with a threshold of 10^-3, where using a full initial condition including velocity, gravity, and density fields shows a greater effect on the transition of halos from bound to unbound state, as opposed to using only the initial density field.
